title: POCUS Guide
sources: Critical Vector — POCUS Master Guide (original content, 18 sections)

changelog.change: Rewritten from the Critical Vector POCUS Master Guide — exam-by-exam diagnostic anchors for FoCUS, lung, eFAST, IVC, RUSH shock, DVT, and procedural guidance. Cleared the placeholder/licensing flags.

summary: Probe and view selection by clinical question, with the diagnostic anchors for each focused exam. Answers focused binary questions — not a substitute for a comprehensive study.

items: Phased array (1-5 MHz) — cardiac, and any deep window through rib spaces.
Curvilinear (2-5 MHz) — abdominal, eFAST, IVC, lung (deep), aorta.
Linear (7-15 MHz) — vascular access, DVT, lung sliding / pneumothorax, soft tissue, ocular, nerve.
Rule: use the highest frequency that still penetrates to the target — resolution degrades with depth.
Views: parasternal long (PLAX), parasternal short, apical 4-chamber (A4C), subcostal 4-chamber (SC4C) + IVC.
EF gestalt — visual: normal / mildly reduced / moderately reduced / severely reduced. EPSS (E-point septal separation) > 7 mm suggests a reduced EF; > 13 mm is markedly reduced.

RV assessment — RV:LV end-diastolic diameter > 1 (apical) or a D-shaped septum = RV pressure/volume overload; with hypotension + this pattern, think acute PE. McConnell's sign (RV free-wall akinesis with apical sparing) is specific for acute PE.
Pericardial effusion — anechoic stripe that tracks circumferentially and moves with the heart (vs. pleural effusion, which sits posterior to the descending aorta on PLAX).
Tamponade — physiology, not size: diastolic RV collapse, systolic RA collapse, a plethoric non-collapsing IVC, and respirophasic mitral/tricuspid inflow variation.

body.text: Subcostal long axis, measure ~2 cm from the RA junction. A small, > 50% collapsing IVC suggests low filling pressure / fluid tolerance; a plethoric, non-collapsing IVC suggests high right-sided pressure (tamponade, RV failure, tension physiology, volume overload). IVC is one data point — integrate with the lung and cardiac exams; it does not predict fluid responsiveness on its own.

items: Normal: lung sliding present + A-lines (horizontal reverberation) + ≤ 2 B-lines per zone.

Pneumothorax: absent lung sliding + absent B-lines + a 'lung point' (the transition where sliding reappears) is pathognomonic. M-mode 'barcode/stratosphere' sign replaces the 'seashore' sign. Absent sliding alone is not enough (bullae, prior pleurodesis, mainstem intubation, ARDS).
Cardiogenic pulmonary edema: bilateral, gravity-dependent B-lines (≥ 3 per zone), smooth pleural line, often with effusions.
Consolidation: tissue-like ('hepatization') lung with air bronchograms; ± shred sign at the border.
Pleural effusion: anechoic space above the diaphragm, spine sign (vertebrae visible above the diaphragm), plankton/swirling in exudates.
BLUE protocol: A-profile + DVT → PE; A-profile, no DVT, lung point → pneumothorax; B-profile → pulmonary edema; A/B or C profile with fever → pneumonia.
Views: RUQ (Morrison's / hepatorenal), LUQ (splenorenal + subphrenic), pelvis (retrovesical / pouch of Douglas), subxiphoid cardiac; extended = bilateral anterior lung for pneumothorax.
Positive = anechoic free fluid in a dependent recess. RUQ is the most sensitive single view for hemoperitoneum. A negative eFAST does not exclude injury — repeat it, or go to CT if stable.
Pericardial fluid + hypotension after penetrating trauma → OR / pericardiotomy, not a drain.

rows: Flat IVC, A-lines, + free fluid (eFAST) or AAA
Effusion with collapse / RV strain / hyperdynamic small LV
Plethoric IVC; absent lung sliding (tension PTX)

body.text: Linear probe, transverse. Compress the common femoral vein (at and just below the saphenofemoral junction) and the popliteal vein (popliteal fossa); some protocols add the femoral vein along the adductor canal. Full coaptation of the vein walls = no DVT at that level. Non-compressible = acute DVT. Do not use colour/spectral Doppler as the primary test — compression is the standard.

items: Central line — short-axis for the initial survey (vein medial/compressible, artery lateral/pulsatile/non-compressible), then long-axis or dynamic-needle-tip tracking for the puncture; confirm the wire in the vein before dilating.
Arterial line / difficult IV — long-axis, shallow angle, walk the tip to the anterior wall.
Thoracentesis / paracentesis — mark the largest pocket with the patient in the position they'll be tapped in; identify the diaphragm, liver/spleen, and bowel to avoid.
Pericardiocentesis — apical or subxiphoid, whichever is closest to the skin with no lung/liver in the path; agitated-saline confirmation.
LP — mark the midline and the interspace, measure skin-to-ligamentum depth (helpful in obesity).
Airway — bilateral lung sliding + no gastric 'double-tract' sign after intubation supports tracheal placement; identify the cricothyroid membrane pre-emptively in a predicted difficult airway.
